evaluation.positioning_hook: A Silicon Valley founder and his lawyer wife let a seductive “unicorn” into their marriage, then discover she’s weaponizing desire, blackmail, and murder to keep them hooked.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and saleable: a marriage, a seductress, blackmail, and a murder cover-up. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant thriller because the erotic material and relationship focus skew adult, but the hook is strong enough to travel.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly at the gala and beach-house sequence: a couple is drawn into a third who turns out to be dangerous. The title concept is also baked into the plot, which gives the premise a strong, easy-to-pitch identity.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Tom and Liz are a credible, conflicted pair with enough history to carry the movie, and Aria is a vivid disruptor with real screen presence. They’re compelling, but the script is built more on dynamic than on deep individual reinvention.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to a psychosexual triangle inside the Silicon Valley elite, and it uses the “unicorn” subculture as a narrative engine rather than a backdrop. The tonal confidence in the sex scenes, social satire, and thriller escalation gives it a sharper edge than a standard affair thriller.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps tightening the noose: gala flirtation, first threesome, stalking texts, blackmail, Mike’s death, Benny’s death, and the final trap. Each escalation is tied to a concrete consequence, so the movie keeps generating forward pressure.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The central idea feels fresh because it fuses marriage drama, tech-world status anxiety, and a predatory sexual arrangement into one engine. The reveal that Aria is not just a seductress but a long-game manipulator gives the premise a memorable, inevitable twist.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Silicon Valley gala culture, Oakland art scene, Acorn projects, and Stinson Beach domesticity create a specific social map with class tension baked in. It’s not a sprawling world, but it’s textured enough to feel lived-in and story-generating.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct erotic-thriller register: glossy, intimate, then increasingly poisonous. The contrast between polished wealth and raw sexual danger is consistent and recognizable throughout.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real undercurrents here around marriage fatigue, class resentment, and the hunger to feel chosen. The final Aria childhood-fire image adds a deeper psychological layer, though the movie mostly plays its hand rather than withholding for long.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Tom, Liz, Aria, Mike, Benny, and Justin all generate usable tension in different combinations, and the script repeatedly reconfigures those relationships. The triangle is the engine, but the supporting players keep the pressure from feeling static.

lead_characters.name: Tom Chase
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-30s, white, Silicon Valley founder, married father
lead_characters.hook: Tom is the polished-but-not-quite-native tech founder who thinks he’s buying control, status, and a future, only to discover he’s emotionally outmatched by the people around him. He’s handsome, decent, and self-protective, which makes him believable as both a husband and a man who can be seduced by the promise of being seen.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a Matthew McConaughey in True Detective-style role: controlled charisma, sexual unease, and a man whose confidence slowly cracks under pressure. It gives an actor the chance to play charm, shame, jealousy, and panic in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Liz Chase
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-30s, white, lawyer, wife, mother
lead_characters.hook: Liz is the sharper, more emotionally literate half of the marriage, and the script keeps revealing how much of her composure is professional armor. She’s not just reacting to Tom and Aria; she’s the one who most clearly understands the cost of what’s happening, which gives her real authority even when she’s destabilized.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Laura Linney in Ozark or Nicole Kidman in Big Little Lies so much traction: intelligence, restraint, and a buried volatility that finally breaks through. It offers a strong actress the chance to move from controlled professional to morally compromised co-conspirator.

lead_characters.name: Aria Greene
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s, ambiguous ethnicity, artist, lower-income background
lead_characters.hook: Aria is the movie’s seductive engine: part fantasy projection, part predator, part wounded survivor, and eventually something much darker. She performs confidence like a weapon, but the script keeps letting us glimpse the need, rage, and damage underneath it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a breakout-vehicle role in the vein of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve or Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl: alluring, dangerous, and constantly shifting the audience’s allegiance. It gives an actor the rare chance to be erotic, funny, manipulative, and terrifying without losing control of the frame.

lead_characters.name: Mike Kreski
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 40s, operator, wealth manager / deal intermediary
lead_characters.hook: Mike is the slick Silicon Valley fixer who understands the social game better than Tom does and quietly helps steer the whole machine. He reads as comic relief at first, but the script uses him as a pressure valve and a key piece of the conspiracy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play charm with rot underneath, like a Paul Dano or Jon Hamm type of part in a prestige thriller. It’s a scene-stealing supporting turn with real narrative consequence.

lead_characters.name: Benny Taylor
lead_characters.hook: Benny is Aria’s damaged enforcer and ex-lover, but the script keeps him human enough that he never becomes a pure thug. He’s jealous, vulnerable, and trapped in the orbit of someone he can’t escape, which makes him more than just a plot device.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting territory for an actor who can play menace and hurt at once, the kind of role that gives a performer a memorable, volatile second gear. It’s the sort of part that can break out in a thriller if cast with real edge.

lead_characters.name: Justin Chase
lead_characters.hook: Justin starts as the grounded family anchor and becomes the most alarming collateral damage in the story. The script uses him to raise the stakes from adult infidelity to something far more personal and dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong young-actor role because it shifts from breezy teen confidence to real vulnerability and shock. It gives a performer a late-film emotional turn that matters to the whole story.

lead_characters.name: Leo Vitulo
lead_characters.hook: Leo is the calm, competent adult in the room, the guy who can actually read the situation without getting seduced by it. He functions as the movie’s procedural ballast and gives the final act a credible investigative spine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, authoritative supporting role that actors like Shea Whigham or Michael Shannon can make feel bigger than the page count. It’s a clean, professional showcase for controlled intensity.

lead_characters.name: Charles Stone
lead_characters.hook: Charles is the polished, predatory money figure who embodies the status world Tom wants into. He’s not a villain in a traditional sense, but he’s a cold reminder that the whole ecosystem is transactional.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is premium supporting material for an actor who can play wealth as menace, like a Succession-style power player. It gives a performer a few sharp scenes with real authority and social dominance.

lead_characters.name: Edith von Strick
lead_characters.hook: Edith is a small but useful emblem of the conservative, reputation-conscious world Liz serves. She helps show the professional stakes around Liz’s public image and the kind of clients that could be endangered by scandal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a crisp character-actor cameo with a specific social register, the sort of role that lets a veteran performer land instant class and authority. It’s not a showy part, but it’s sharply defined.

lead female role requires strong erotic and emotional range
Aria needs a highly specific mix of glamour, danger, and vulnerability
supporting roles skew 40s-70s professional and affluent

technical.vfx_details: No visible VFX requirement beyond basic cleanup and possible security-camera inserts.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical fire imagery in the opening flashback, a smashed phone, a broken glass injury, and a vandalized house exterior.

rights_flags.detail: Robyn & Röyksopp 'Do It Again', FKA twigs 'Two Weeks', James Blake 'The Wilhelm Scream', Skeeter Davis 'The End of the World'

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult psychosexual thriller with prestige-drama packaging and a streamer-friendly erotic edge.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the script spans multiple distinct locations, several night exteriors, a beach-house sequence, a club/parking-structure set, and a practical fire opening that all need to be scoped cleanly.

casting.note: Aria is the hardest lift: she has to be seductive, funny, manipulative, emotionally damaged, and credible in both erotic and threatening modes. Tom and Liz also need actors who can sell a marriage with real history, not just plot mechanics.

development.note: The movie’s engine is clear, but the final-act reveal around Justin and the moral line around Aria’s manipulation make the audience contract sensitive. The script is strongest when it stays in the triangle; the broader conspiracy material is functional but less distinctive.

comp_set.title: Fatal Attraction
comp_set.why_it_comps: The domestic affair-to-threat escalation and the sense of a seductive outsider turning a marriage into a danger zone are the same core engine.

comp_set.title: Gone Girl
comp_set.why_it_comps: It shares the marriage-as-performance pressure, the weaponized intimacy, and the way a couple’s private life becomes public leverage.

comp_set.title: The Invitation
comp_set.why_it_comps: The social gathering that slowly reveals itself as a trap, plus the escalating unease around who is manipulating whom, is very much in that lane.

comp_set.title: The Last Thing He Wanted
comp_set.why_it_comps: The blend of adult political/wealth-world intrigue with a female character whose motives are harder to pin down fits the same adult-thriller lane.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like sexy, high-stakes relationship thrillers where desire and danger are inseparable.
audience_target.demographics: 35-54 skew, slightly female-leaning but viable for couples viewing; upscale streamer audience, prestige-thriller fans, and viewers drawn to marriage-under-pressure stories.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary settings, limited company size, and no heavy VFX keep it in indie feature territory, though the night shoots, beach house, and multiple upscale locations will want disciplined scheduling.

types_of_buyers: indie producers looking for actor-driven elevated genre
director-driven companies with a prestige-suspense mandate
lane_fit.detail: This sits in the lane where adult sexuality, class tension, and psychological danger are the selling points rather than the garnish. The script is built for buyers who want a contained, actor-forward thriller with a sharp hook and a premium finish.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The story resolves its central triangle and murder cover-up cleanly, and there is no clear franchise or spinoff vector beyond this one narrative.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The title concept is the movie.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has a clean, ownable hook that can be sold in one sentence and understood immediately by buyers. That makes it unusually easy to position for streamer acquisition or a director-led package. It’s the kind of premise that attracts adult-thriller audiences and actors who want a bold, high-concept role.
strengths.evidence: Aria explicitly defines herself as a 'Unicorn,' and the entire plot turns on what that means inside the marriage.

strengths.what_it_means: Tom, Liz, and Aria create a three-way dynamic that keeps reconfiguring power, desire, and blame, which is exactly what makes relationship thrillers sticky. That gives the project a strong word-of-mouth engine for adult audiences and a clear showcase for three actors.
strengths.evidence: The gala flirtation, beach-house threesome, office hookup, and final trap all escalate from the same relational triangle.

strengths.dimension_or_area: It has a premium erotic-thriller lane.
strengths.what_it_means: The script knows what kind of movie it is and commits to it without apology, which is a real asset in a market that still buys adult suspense when the hook is sharp. That makes it attractive to streamers and financiers looking for a polished, sexy, actor-driven genre play.
strengths.evidence: The Robyn, FKA twigs, and James Blake needle drops, plus the explicit seduction scenes, give it a clear adult register.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The class contrast gives the story bite.
strengths.what_it_means: The move between Silicon Valley wealth, Oakland grit, and the Acorn projects gives the thriller a social texture that lifts it beyond a generic affair story. Buyers looking for prestige genre with a real-world edge will respond to that built-in class tension.
strengths.evidence: The gala, the Oakland gallery, Benny’s apartment, and Aria’s neighborhood all sit in different social worlds.

strengths.what_it_means: The character is written to be magnetic, dangerous, and unstable in a way that can launch an actor’s profile if cast correctly. That kind of role is a real packaging asset because it can pull in talent who want a scene-stealing, conversation-starting part.
strengths.evidence: Aria moves from seductive artist to manipulator to violent threat, while still keeping the audience guessing.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending lands on consequence, not just shock.
strengths.what_it_means: The final act resolves the danger through a moral and legal trap, which gives the movie a satisfying aftertaste instead of a simple body-count finish. That makes it easier to sell as a prestige thriller rather than disposable genre.
strengths.evidence: The knife, the video statement, the police cleanup, and the final family tableau all tie the climax back to the marriage and the sale.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept prestige erotic thriller with a title that tells you exactly what the movie is, and a triangle that keeps escalating into blackmail, murder, and moral collapse. It’s commercially attractive because it’s contemporary, actor-forward, and contained enough to package without tentpole economics.

items.area: Aria’s psychology gets very broad in the back half.
items.detail: The script gives her a strong seductive persona, but once the blackmail and murder mechanics kick in, she starts to read more as a plot engine than a fully legible person. That’s not a deal-breaker for the genre, but it does make the final stretch more dependent on performance than on page-level inevitability.

items.area: The final-act Justin reveal is a hard tonal turn.
items.detail: The move from adult psychosexual manipulation to the revelation that Aria has been texting and seducing the teenage son is a major escalation that will narrow the audience and raise sensitivity questions. It’s the sharpest audience-risk moment in the script because it changes the movie’s moral temperature very quickly.

items.area: The music budget is not incidental.
items.detail: Robyn & Röyksopp, FKA twigs, James Blake, and Skeeter Davis are all specifically named and materially shape the movie’s tone. Those are real clearance and sync-cost items, not placeholders, and they need to be treated as part of the package rather than as optional flavor.

items.area: Aria is a narrow casting lane.
items.detail: The role has to sell erotic power, class intelligence, menace, and emotional damage without losing control of the frame. That is a real casting filter, and the movie’s marketability rises or falls on whether the right actor can make her feel irresistible before she becomes alarming.

items.area: The thriller depends on a lot of coincidence.
items.detail: Mike knowing Aria, Aria finding the couple at the gala, the repeated reappearances, and the final convergence at the beach house all require the audience to accept a fairly engineered chain of events. The script sells it with confidence, but a buyer will still notice how much of the engine is driven by coincidence and access.

issues.headline: The movie’s biggest commercial risk is that the back half gets more extreme and more engineered just as it needs to stay seductive and inevitable. The music clearances and the Aria casting lift are manageable, but the Justin turn is the moment every buyer will clock as the point where the audience contract gets much more sensitive.
